items.prompt: Why does day length change through the year?

options.label: The Earth's axis is tilted
options.feedback: Each hemisphere leans towards the Sun in turn.

options.label: The Earth's orbit is a long oval
options.feedback: It is very nearly a circle, and that is not the cause.

options.label: The Sun shines harder in summer
options.feedback: Its output barely varies at all.

options.label: The Earth spins faster in summer
options.feedback: The spin rate is essentially constant.

items.ok_line: A tilt of 23.5 degrees explains the whole calendar.
items.ko_line: When it is summer here it is winter in Australia. Distance cannot explain that.
items.exp_text: The Earth's axis leans about 23.5 degrees from the upright, and it keeps pointing the same way all year. For half the orbit the northern hemisphere leans sunward and receives longer days and more direct light; for the other half it leans away. The tilt explains why the two hemispheres have opposite seasons — something distance from the Sun could never do, since both are the same distance at once.

items.prompt: What happens at the summer solstice?

options.label: The longest day of the year
options.feedback: The Sun reaches its highest point at noon.

options.label: Day and night are equal
options.feedback: That is an equinox, six weeks earlier or later.

options.label: The Earth is nearest the Sun
options.feedback: That happens in January, regardless of season.

options.label: The Earth's axis briefly straightens
options.feedback: The tilt never changes through the year.

items.ok_line: The Sun at its highest, and the day at its longest.
items.ko_line: Solstice means the Sun standing still. Standing still where?
items.exp_text: At the solstice one hemisphere leans as far towards the Sun as it ever does, giving the longest day and the highest noon Sun. The name means sun-stands-still: for a few days around it the noon altitude barely changes before reversing. In the far north the Sun does not set at all; south of the equator the same date is the shortest day of winter.

options.label: When day and night are nearly equal
options.feedback: The Sun rises due east and sets due west.

options.label: The longest day of the year
options.feedback: That is the summer solstice.

options.label: When the Earth is furthest from the Sun
options.feedback: That falls in July, unconnected to the equinox.

options.label: When the Moon crosses the Sun
options.feedback: That is an eclipse, and unrelated.

items.ok_line: Equal night, which is what the word says.
items.ko_line: The word comes from the Latin for equal night.
items.exp_title: The two days that belong to everyone
items.exp_text: Twice a year the Earth's tilt lies sideways to the Sun, neither hemisphere leaning towards it, and both receive close to twelve hours of light. On those days the Sun rises due east and sets due west from every point on the planet, and the two poles each see it skimming the horizon. Day and night are not exactly equal, because the atmosphere lifts the Sun's image and daylight is counted from the disc's upper edge.

items.prompt: Why is the hottest weather several weeks after the longest day?

options.label: Land and sea take time to warm
options.feedback: Heat keeps accumulating after the peak sunlight.

options.label: The Sun grows stronger in August
options.feedback: It is already past its highest point by then.

options.label: The Earth moves closer in summer
options.feedback: It is furthest from the Sun in July.

options.label: Days keep lengthening after the solstice
options.feedback: They start shortening immediately after it.

items.ok_line: Heat piles up as long as more arrives than escapes.
items.ko_line: A pan does not reach its hottest the instant the flame is highest.
items.exp_title: The lag of a warming world
items.exp_text: Peak sunlight arrives at the solstice, but the ground and especially the oceans keep absorbing more than they radiate for weeks afterwards, so temperatures go on climbing until the balance tips. The delay runs about four to six weeks on land and longer by the sea. The same lag appears each day on a small scale: the hottest hour is mid-afternoon, not noon.

items.prompt: How does day length vary at the equator through the year?

options.label: Hardly at all
options.feedback: About twelve hours of light every day of the year.

options.label: By several hours
options.feedback: That variation belongs to higher latitudes.

options.label: More than anywhere else
options.feedback: The equator varies least of anywhere.

options.label: It reverses twice a year
options.feedback: Nothing reverses. It simply stays steady.

items.ok_line: Twelve hours, every day, all year.
items.ko_line: The tilt affects the poles most. What does that mean for the middle?
items.exp_text: The tilt swings the poles in and out of sunlight dramatically, but at the equator its effect nearly cancels: daylight there varies by only a few minutes across the whole year. The Sun rises steeply, passes almost overhead and sets steeply, giving very short twilights. Seasons near the equator are marked by rain rather than by light or temperature — a wet season and a dry one, not a summer and a winter.

items.prompt: Why is summer warmer than winter?

options.label: Sunlight strikes at a steeper angle
options.feedback: The same energy is concentrated on less ground.

options.label: The Earth is nearer the Sun
options.feedback: It is actually further away during northern summer.

options.label: The Sun burns hotter in summer
options.feedback: Its output is essentially constant.

options.label: The atmosphere thins in summer
options.feedback: Air thickness does not change with season.

items.ok_line: Same beam, smaller patch, more heat per square metre.
items.ko_line: Shine a torch straight down on a table, then at a slant. Which patch is brighter?
items.exp_text: Two things work together. A high Sun delivers its energy nearly straight down, so a given beam covers a small patch of ground and heats it strongly; a low Sun spreads the same beam across a much larger area. On top of that, summer days are longer, so the heating runs for more hours and the night has less time to undo it. The angle matters more than the length.

items.prompt: Why does the Sun rise at a different point on the horizon through the year?

options.label: Its path shifts with the tilt
options.feedback: North of east in summer, south of east in winter.

options.label: The Earth wobbles from day to day
options.feedback: The axis is remarkably steady over a year.

options.label: The horizon itself moves
options.feedback: The horizon is fixed by the ground you stand on.

options.label: The Sun drifts among the stars
options.feedback: It does, but that is not what moves the rising point.

items.ok_line: The rising point swings north and south with the season.
items.ko_line: It rises due east only twice a year. What is different on the other days?
items.exp_title: A swing you can mark on the ground
items.exp_text: The Sun rises due east only at the equinoxes. Through summer it rises well north of east and sets north of west, and the whole arc is higher and longer; in winter it does the reverse. The swing is wide enough to be marked with stones, which is exactly what Stonehenge and many other alignments do — they are calendars built by watching where the Sun comes up.

items.prompt: What happens at the poles at the equinox?

options.label: The Sun sits on the horizon
options.feedback: It circles the rim, neither rising nor setting.

options.label: The Sun passes directly overhead
options.feedback: It never rises high at the poles at any date.

options.label: Day and night alternate hourly
options.feedback: Nothing alternates. There is one long transition.

options.label: Complete darkness falls for a day
options.feedback: It is the moment light returns, not the reverse.

items.ok_line: Six months of day ending, six months of night beginning.
items.ko_line: At the pole the Sun circles rather than rises. Where is it circling at the equinox?
items.exp_text: At a pole the Sun does not rise and set daily; it spirals slowly upward for six months and slowly down for the next six. The equinox is the moment it crosses the horizon, so each pole has exactly one sunrise and one sunset per year, each taking days to complete. It is why polar research stations mark the equinox rather than any particular morning.

items.prompt: Why does the earliest sunset not fall on the shortest day?

options.label: Solar noon drifts through the year
options.feedback: It shifts by minutes, moving sunrise and sunset unevenly.

options.label: Clocks are set slightly wrong
options.feedback: The effect appears with perfectly accurate clocks.

options.label: The Earth speeds up in December
options.feedback: Its spin does not vary in that way.

options.label: Twilight lasts longer in winter
options.feedback: Twilight length does not move the moment of sunset.

items.ok_line: The day is shortest at the solstice, but noon itself keeps sliding.
items.ko_line: Sunset and sunrise are measured from noon. What if noon is not fixed?
items.exp_title: Noon is not where the clock says
items.exp_text: The Earth's orbit is slightly oval and its axis is tilted, so the true solar noon drifts back and forth against clock time by up to sixteen minutes across the year. In December that drift is running fast enough that the earliest sunset falls roughly a fortnight before the solstice and the latest sunrise a fortnight after. The shortest day is still the solstice — but its two ends do not arrive together.

items.prompt: What would happen to the seasons if the Earth's axis were upright?

options.label: They would disappear
options.feedback: Every latitude would get the same light all year.

options.label: They would swap over
options.feedback: There would be nothing left to swap.

options.label: They would become more extreme
options.feedback: The tilt is what creates them in the first place.

options.label: Only winter would remain
options.feedback: Nothing would single out one season.

items.ok_line: No tilt, no seasons. Twelve-hour days everywhere, forever.
items.ko_line: Remove the cause and ask what is left of the effect.
items.exp_title: The tilt is the whole story
items.exp_text: With an upright axis every place on Earth would receive twelve hours of daylight every day, and the Sun would follow the same path all year. Climate would be banded by latitude and never change: permanent warmth at the equator, permanent cold at the poles, no spring and no harvest season. Uranus shows the opposite extreme — tipped on its side, each pole faces the Sun for about 42 years at a stretch.
